1:
The opening particle they all take as looking back. Robertson says it points to the triumphant note closing the preceding chapter after the despair before it; Ellicott, that the Apostle had there touched the confines of the deliverance he now describes; Wesley, that the thread interrupted earlier is resumed, and he comes now to liberty. Calvin explains that after describing the contest the godly have with their own flesh he returns to the consolation, joining three things: the imperfection under which the faithful always labour, the mercy of God in pardoning it, and the regeneration of the Spirit, set there so that no one should flatter himself. Gill says that having discoursed on the inward struggle, the apostle now notices the solid ground of spiritual peace; Barnes, that the chapter is designed to show the gospel effecting what the law could not. Henry calls the verse a triumph after that melancholy conflict, sin remaining and vexing but not ruining; the complaint the apostle takes to himself, the comfort he transfers to all true believers.

On the removal of condemnation Ellicott is precise: what is removed is the condemnation which in God's present and final judgment impends over the sinner, and it is removed by the intervention of Christ and the believer's union with him. Robertson puts it bluntly: as sinners we deserved condemnation in spite of the struggle, but God offers pardon to those in Christ Jesus; the fire has burned on and around the Cross, and there alone is safety. Wesley extends it both ways, for things present or past. Theodoret gives the reason from experience, that our passions can no longer master us without our own consent, now that grace is received.

The phrase that follows Gill calls of difficult interpretation. He allows it of the Gospel declaring deliverance from the law of Moses, and defends calling the Gospel a law, not as succeeding the law of works nor as requiring conditions, but as a doctrine and ordered chain of truths. Clarke presses the contrast: the law was a spirit of death, binding those under it to condemnation, while the Gospel is not only a rule of life but the sovereign energy by which guilt is removed and sin's power broken, so that what the law bound unto death it looses unto life eternal. Wesley says the law of the Spirit is the gospel, that of sin and death the Mosaic dispensation.

Barnes and Robertson both refer the word Spirit to the Holy Spirit, Barnes explaining that law here means the rule the Spirit of life exerts, Robertson calling it the authority exercised by the Holy Spirit, who bestows life and rests in Christ Jesus; two chief manuscripts, he notes, read thee rather than me, and it matters little. Ellicott calls the verse a statement of the great antithesis of which the rest of the section is a development: union with Christ imparts the Spirit of Christ, this Spirit creates within the believer a law, and the result of that law is life. Calvin grants that the language is not strictly correct, since by law the apostle designates the Spirit of God, and takes the genitive after the Hebrew manner as an adjective, life-giving; whence they who detain a man in the letter expose him to death. Theodoret sets the two laws side by side, that as the apostle had just called sin the law of sin so now he calls the life-giving Spirit the law of the spirit of life, and finds a double freedom, since grace has overthrown the power of sin and ended the tyranny of death. Lightfoot's note here looks ahead rather than at the words in hand, arguing of the term rendered vanity later in the chapter that it denotes not the vanishing outward state but the inward emptiness of mind, as when the Gentiles became vain in their imaginations.
3:
What the law could not do they define by ruling out a fault in the law itself. Barnes says the failing was not in the law, which was good, but in the strength of the natural passions and the sinfulness of the unrenewed heart. Clarke lists the impossibilities: the law could not pardon, could not sanctify, and could not dispense with its own requisitions, being the rule of righteousness and bound to condemn unrighteousness; had obedience been perfect it would have rewarded, but transgression having taken place it was rendered inefficient. Theodoret says the law was not evil but good, though impotent, its injunctions having been given to men encumbered with a mortal nature. Gill excludes the law of the mind and the ceremonial law before settling on the moral law. Robertson renders the opening as the impossibility of the law and notes that the phrase has no syntactical connection with the rest of the sentence. Ellicott sets out the whole logic in a sentence: precisely where the law of Moses showed its impotence God interposed, so that the flesh, the scene of sin's former triumphs, became the scene of its defeat.

The words about the likeness are handled with care. Theodoret is the most exact: the apostle says not in the likeness of flesh but in the likeness of sinful flesh, for the Son received actually the human nature but human sin he received not, so that likeness qualifies the sinfulness and not the flesh. Robertson makes the same distinction grammatically, that the genitives mean flesh marked by sin, true of man's flesh but not of Christ's, and adds that it is a real man though more than man, God's own Son. Wesley states the exchange plainly: we with our sinful flesh were devoted to death, but God sending his own Son in the likeness of that flesh, though pure from sin, condemned the sin in our flesh and gave sentence that it should be destroyed. Ellicott takes the sending as both in a body of flesh like that in which sin resides and as an offering to expiate human sin.

The clause about the righteousness of the law fulfilled divides them sharply. Calvin will not allow it to describe anything the believer does: those who understand that the renewed fulfil the law by the Spirit of Christ introduce a gloss wholly alien to the meaning of Paul, since the faithful never make such proficiency here that the justification of the law becomes complete in them. It must be applied to forgiveness, the obedience of Christ being accepted for us so that the law is satisfied and we are counted just, its rigour no longer able to condemn. Gill reaches the same place by another route, taking the law's demand of active obedience and holding that by Christ's obedience we are made righteous. Theodoret combines both, that Christ paid our debt and fulfilled what the law aimed at, concluding that the law deserves praise, not blame.

Against this Ellicott reads the clause of an actual change: hitherto the law could not be kept because of the antagonistic influence of the flesh, but henceforth it may be, that influence having ceased and the Spirit's taken its place, so that we might be examples of its fulfilment. Clarke takes both halves together, that guilt might be pardoned through the merit of the sacrifice and that we might be enabled by his grace to walk in newness of life. Barnes reads it of conformity and obedience. Wesley takes it of the holiness the law required, and observes that from this point the apostle describes primarily the state of believers, that of unbelievers only to illustrate it. Robertson parses the purpose clause, says Christ met the requirement in our stead, and calls the two ways of walking the two laws of life set against each other in this chapter and the last.
5:
Being after the flesh they distinguish from having flesh. Gill insists that not all who have flesh in them are meant, since the best of saints have it and grace does not remove it; there is a difference between being in the flesh, being after it, and flesh being in us. Barnes takes them as the unrenewed. Ellicott sharpens it: these are men who not only direct their conduct by the promptings of the flesh but are, in the whole bent of their dispositions, the slaves of them. Wesley names what the cravings fix upon, pleasure, praise, or riches; Clarke makes the contrast historical, between the Jews and genuine Christians; Robertson glosses the verb as putting the mind on a thing. Theodoret takes the Spirit as the grace of the Spirit and draws the rule that he who follows it both thinks and does the things agreeable to it. Calvin explains why the antithesis is introduced: not only to confirm what precedes by an argument from its opposite, but to relieve the faithful with a seasonable consolation, lest, conscious of many infirmities, they should despair.

On the word rendered carnally minded Calvin reviews the renderings. Erasmus gave affection and the old translator prudence, but since the apostle's term answers to what Moses calls the imagination of the heart and takes in all the faculties of the soul, Calvin judges minding the more suitable. Gill reaches the same breadth by enumeration, the phrase including mind, judgment, will, affections and reasonings, and may be rendered the wisdom of the flesh. Robertson calls it the bent of the flesh; Theodoret notes that the apostle says not the flesh but the inclination of the flesh, the breaking forth of the passions.

That such minding is death rather than merely deserving it is pressed by several. Barnes calls the expression one of great energy, since this not only leads to death but is death itself. Ellicott says the same, that to think of nothing but the gratification of the senses is in itself that dead condition of soul which issues in eternal death, while thoughts governed by the Spirit bring a vital harmony of the soul's functions. Wesley calls it the sure mark of spiritual death, and the peace answering it the foretaste of life everlasting.

The enmity they take at full strength. Gill directs it against the being of God, since the carnal mind reasons against it, wishes he were not, and would bury him in forgetfulness. Clarke calls it irreconcilable and implacable hatred, and explains the impossibility that follows by saying the carnal mind will come under no obedience because it is itself sin and the very principle of rebellion. Theodoret puts the point as a question, how one who has admitted the tyranny of the passions should embrace God's service while still choosing to serve sin. Robertson notes that the verb is a military term for subjection to orders and that the present tense marks continued insubordination. Wesley directs the enmity against God's existence, power and providence; Ellicott compresses the whole into a syllogism, that the carnal mind is death because it implies enmity with God, and enmity with God is death.

On the conclusion Calvin says he rendered the adversative as an illative, since the apostle infers that all who give themselves to the lusts of the flesh are abominable before God, and all who walk not after the Spirit are alienated from Christ, being without spiritual life. Clarke draws the consequence that if they cannot please God they must be displeasing to him. Barnes limits the impossibility to the condition, that while they pursue their corrupt desires they cannot please him. Robertson enters the necessary caution: this does not mean the sinner has no responsibility and cannot be saved, for he is responsible and can be saved by the change of heart through the Holy Spirit.
9:
Gill takes the turn as a change of address: these are not carnal but spiritual men, no longer in unregeneracy but in a state of grace. Theodoret guards the words from misreading: those who received these instructions were not devoid of the body, but were conquerors over the fleshly passions, as our Lord says his disciples are not of the world though they did not come from elsewhere. Clarke notes the reversal, that the sinful principle had dwelt in them before and its motions proved its indwelling. Calvin observes that a general truth is applied hypothetically to the readers, so that they might gather with certainty that they were of the number from whom Christ had taken away the curse. Wesley glosses being in the Spirit as being under his government.

Ellicott observes that the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are used interchangeably, the Spirit of Christ being the presence of Christ himself in the soul. Robertson says the second phrase means the same as the first and finds in the interchange an incidental argument for the deity of Christ; what is taught is neither Pantheism nor Buddhism but the mystical union of the believer with Christ. Cyril of Jerusalem multiplies the titles, showing that the Holy Spirit and the Comforter are one, and the Comforter the same as the Spirit of Truth. Wesley is severe on the closing sentence: a plain declaration admitting no exception.

The indwelling of Christ they qualify carefully. Gill distinguishes it from the presence by which Christ fills the world: his person is in heaven, his blood within the veil, his righteousness upon his people, his Spirit and grace within them. Barnes calls the expression figurative, since literally Christ cannot be in a Christian. Henry states the equivalence in a line: if the Spirit be in us Christ is in us, dwelling in the heart by faith. Calvin says what was affirmed of the Spirit is now affirmed of Christ, to intimate the mode of his dwelling in us; and the children of God are counted spiritual not on the ground of complete perfection but of the newness of life begun in them.

On the body being dead Ellicott takes the word of physical death and marks the limit: the doom entailed by sin still attaches to the body, but only to the body, and there sin's hold on the Christian ends. Robertson says it has the seeds of death in it, and calls the spirit answering it God-begotten life. Theodoret says the apostle makes clear what had been ambiguous, showing that it was not the flesh he condemns but sin, since he bids the body be dead to sin. Clarke offers both readings, that the members no more perform sin's work than a corpse performs natural functions, or that the life of man is forfeited. Wesley says the body is devoted to death for sin heretofore committed, the spirit already truly alive.

The last verse is an argument from the resurrection. Barnes grounds it on two things, the power of God and the connexion between Christ and his people, since he who did restore Christ to life will also restore them. Calvin calls it a confirmation drawn from the efficient cause, and holds that in Christ was exhibited a specimen of the power belonging to the whole Church. Clarke makes the resurrection of Christ the pattern after which they shall be raised. Gill insists that the quickening is not sanctification, since mortal bodies are spoken of. Theodoret says the apostle invigorates them by hope and inspires a readiness sufficient for present contests, their bodies being before long immortal and superior to the passions that now molest them. On the closing phrase Ellicott judges the authorities to favour the reading because of his Spirit, calling the other an Alexandrian correction, while Robertson allows both and thinks the genitive slightly the likelier.
12:
Chrysostom notices the form of the exhortation. Having shown how great the reward of a spiritual life is, that it makes Christ dwell in us and wings our bodies to heaven, the apostle might have said simply that we ought not to live after the flesh; but he words it more strikingly, saying that we are debtors. Ellicott and Calvin both observe that the second half of the antithesis is left unspoken, so that we are under obligation not to the flesh but, by implication, to the Spirit; Calvin cites Pareus that it was omitted because it was so evident. Barnes sets out three grounds of the obligation: the Spirit dwells in us, his indwelling is designed to purify us, and we have been recovered from the death of sin, so that he who imparted the life may require it be spent in his service. Theodoret says the same briefly: having received salvation and been made partakers of the grace of the Spirit, to him we owe the debt of service. Robertson notes that the negative belongs with the verb, not the infinitive. Gill remarks that the address as brethren rests on a shared spiritual relation and shows the apostle's humility.

The threat that follows Calvin calls a deliberate device, added to shake off their torpor, and turns against a particular error: by it those are confuted who boast of justification by faith without the Spirit of Christ, since there is no confidence in God where there is no love of righteousness. It is true that we are justified through mercy alone, but equally certain that all who are justified are also sanctified. Robertson renders the words as meaning they are on the point of dying, and takes the death as eternal; Clarke allows a temporal death but not exclusively. Theodoret takes it plainly of eternal death, and draws from the second half the superiority of grace over the law: the law points out what is right, grace has the Spirit in addition as a helpmate.

On the mortifying Barnes says it can be done only by the aid of the Holy Ghost, sin being mortified when its power is destroyed. Ellicott renders it as reducing to deadness and atrophy the practices to which our material nature prompts us. Clarke describes it as seeking the grace the Gospel furnishes and resisting, and by resisting mortifying, the deeds of the flesh. Wesley extends the deeds to evil desires and thoughts as well as actions, promising the life of faith here and of glory hereafter. Gill asks whether one who has truly received grace can live after the flesh, and answers that though corrupt nature remains it has not the dominion.

Being led Gill explains by two figures, the leading of the blind and rather of children taught to go, which supposes life in those led and some strength. Barnes makes willingness to yield one evidence of piety, unwillingness a decided evidence of its absence. Clarke says no man without divine assistance can find the way to heaven or walk in it when found, Christ transacting the kingdom's concerns before the throne while the Spirit is the great agent here below. Calvin takes the verse as confirming what precedes: those only are deemed sons of God who are ruled by his Spirit, since by this mark God acknowledges them as his own, and the empty boasting of hypocrites is taken away. Robertson observes that no great distinction can be drawn between the word for son here and the word for child shortly after, since in the highest sense Christ alone is God's Son while in the widest all men are his offspring. Wesley marks the turn in the argument, that the sum is through sufferings to glory. Cyril of Jerusalem, gathering the prophetic titles of the Spirit, insists that he is one and undivided though his operations are various.
15:
The spirit of bondage they are careful not to identify with the Holy Spirit. Gill says it cannot be the Spirit of God, whose character is the reverse, being a Spirit of liberty, and whose office is to show a soul its bondage in order to deliver it. Theodoret is more exact: what is called the spirit of bondage is not the Spirit himself but the imposition of the law as effected by him. Ellicott renders it as such a spirit as slaves would have; Barnes says the slave is under constant fear while the spirit of religion is freedom and confidence. Clarke sets it historically, that all under the law were in bondage to its rites and, transgressing often, were through fear of death subject to bondage. Wesley qualifies it, that the Holy Ghost was not properly a spirit of bondage even under the Old Testament. Calvin turns to the purpose: the Spirit was given not to harass us with trembling, but to calm every perturbation and stir us up to call on God with confidence.

On the cry Wesley notes that the word denotes a vehement speaking with desire and constancy, and that the second title explains the first. Robertson refers the double naming to the child's privilege, and notes that Jews and Gentiles alike receive this adoption. Cyril of Jerusalem sets the Spirit of adoption among the titles of the Holy Ghost, beside the Spirit of holiness and of revelation.

The joint witness they treat with unusual care. Robertson warns that although the noun's gender is neuter, the Greek also used the natural gender, and that it is a grave mistake to call the Holy Spirit it. Calvin observes that the apostle adopts a compound verb rather than saying simply that the Spirit witnesses to our spirit, and holds that our mind, without the Spirit's preceding testimony, could not convey such assurance. Clarke reasons from the other end: the witness cannot be any disposition the adopted person feels, since such a disposition must arise from a knowledge of the adoption which no earthly means can give. Barnes gives three reasons for taking it of the Holy Spirit: this is the natural meaning, the Spirit is the passage's subject, and it would be forced to say of the temper of adoption that it bore witness. Ellicott describes the concurrence: the believer's self-consciousness assures him of his sonship, and besides this he is aware of an objective cause for the feeling. Theodoret takes the first term of the Holy Ghost and the second of the grace of adoption. Wesley calls it a testimony distinct from that of conscience.

On the inheritance Henry marks the difference from human practice, that in earthly inheritances only the firstborn are heirs, whereas the church is a church of the firstborn and all are heirs. Gill compares Roman law, where children inherited whether male or female, with Jewish law, where females inherited only for want of male issue. Clarke presses the object rather than the manner: it is neither an earthly nor a heavenly portion but God himself, since it is not heaven they inherit but God. Calvin argues that since God has adopted us as children he has ordained an inheritance, heavenly and incorruptible, such as Christ possesses. Theodoret observes that since not every son becomes his father's heir, the apostle has done well to join the heirship expressly to the sonship. Robertson calls the compound a late and rare formation found in Philo and in papyri, and notes three such compounds in this verse. Ellicott states the condition without softening it: the Christian has an inheritance of glory to share with Christ, but must not be surprised if before the glory he shares the sufferings, since all who suffer for the gospel suffer with Christ and drink of his cup. Wesley adds that the suffering must be willing and cheerful.
18:
The reckoning they take as a deliberate weighing. Barnes says the verse opens a new division designed to show the power of the gospel in sustaining the soul in trials. Clarke makes the calculation explicit: if the glory to be revealed is the enjoyment of God himself, then the sufferings of this life, which compared with eternity are but for a moment, cannot be put in competition with it, and the case is perfectly clear. Theodoret puts it in a series of balances: the crowns exceed the contests, the reward cannot be set in the same scale with the afflictions, small the affliction but vast the looked-for gain, and therefore what is hoped for is called not payment but glory. Henry sets the two judgments against each other, that the sufferings of the saints strike no deeper than the things of time, and remarks how vastly different are the sentence of the word and the sentiment of the world. Gill takes the present time of the age in which the apostle lived, when God's people suffered much as Christ had foretold. Calvin pauses on the connecting particle, denying that it can be causal since nothing precedes for which a reason is given.

On the glory to be revealed Ellicott prefers upon us to in us, that is, reaching to us and transfiguring us, since the coming of Christ is always conceived as a visible manifestation of glory in those who share it. Robertson says the same, that we shall be included in the radiance of the coming glory, which will put the present sufferings in the shadow. Wesley connects the two clauses, that when that glory is revealed in us the sons of God will be revealed also. Cyril of Jerusalem, whose comment here anticipates a later verse, explains why the Spirit is called the Comforter, because he comforts us and helps our infirmities when we know not what we should pray for as we ought.

What the creature means is the difficulty of the passage, and Clarke says so plainly; he lists six answers that have been given, that it denotes the brute creation, the Jewish people, the godly, the Gentiles, the good angels, or the fallen spirits. Gill reports the view that it means the universe, animate and inanimate, introduced by a rhetorical figure as waiting for a restoration to its paradisiacal estate, but objects that part of the world is afterwards distinguished from it; he mentions also the opinion that angels are meant. Wesley takes it of all visible creatures, believers excepted, all having been sufferers through sin. Calvin omits the various interpretations and understands the passage to mean that there is no element and no part of the world which, touched as it were with a sense of its present misery, does not intensely hope for a resurrection. Theodoret gives the widest list of all: the heaven, the earth, the sea, the air, the sun, the moon, the whole visible creation, and besides these the invisible, angels and archangels and powers and principalities, all waiting for the full perfection of the sons of God.

On the word for expectation they are agreed and delighted. Barnes says it denotes an earnest desire to see an object when the head is thrust forward, an intense anxiety, well employed for the interest with which a Christian looks to his inheritance. Robertson analyses it as a double compound meaning to watch eagerly with outstretched head, notes that the noun is found nowhere but here and in Philippians, and reports Milligan's suggestion that the apostle may have coined it. Ellicott renders it a straining forward with outstretched head, as the crowds outside a race-course strain to see, and adds that our hope is not isolated, the whole creation looking for the same manifestation. Wesley says the word denotes a lively hope of something drawing near.
20:
The question of who is meant divides them three ways. Gill, Lightfoot and Clarke take the creature of the Gentile world. Gill lists what its vanity consisted in, that the Gentiles were without God and Christ, without law or Gospel, and full of vain conceits of their own wisdom, with their philosophy and gross idolatry. Lightfoot and Clarke press a distinction on the two clauses: the Gentile world became vain willingly but was made subject to vanity unwillingly, and they trace this to the confusion of languages at Babel. Barnes takes the creature of the renewed mind, and reads the whole as a reason for its aspiring to adoption's full privileges, the present state not being one it chose. Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Wesley and Theodoret take it of the material creation. Ellicott says the apostle is pointing out what creation is, since if it were perfect there would be no cause for looking hopefully forward. Robertson parses the aorist passive and the rare word for vanity, and says the subjection was due to man's sin though it came by God. Wesley glosses vanity as abuse and corruption, and adds that Adam only made the creation liable to the sentence God pronounced, yet not without hope.

Calvin argues from the opposite side, that since creatures subject to corruption cannot be restored until the sons of God are wholly restored, they long for their own renewal. Theodoret identifies the vanity plainly with corruption, since the next verse speaks of deliverance from the bondage of corruption, and says the visible creation obtained a mortal nature because the Maker of all had foreseen the transgression of man.

On the hope they agree about the punctuation. Gill says the phrase in hope, which our version puts at the end of the one verse, belongs at the head of the next; Clarke and Ellicott make the same connection, Ellicott preferring to render the conjunction that rather than because, citing Meyer. On the word for corruption Lightfoot and Clarke both observe that it very frequently denotes sinful corruption in Scripture, citing corruption through lust. Barnes, reading the creature of the renewed man, makes the ground of hope God's purpose that deliverance shall be granted. Calvin draws a different lesson: it is meet to consider what a dreadful curse we have deserved, since all created things, blameless in themselves, undergo punishment for our sins. Wesley reasons from the word deliverance itself, that destruction is not deliverance, so whatever is destroyed is not delivered at all; the liberty he takes as the state wherein they were created. Robertson says it is the hope of creation and not of the Creator, and quotes Godet that nature has in her unmerited suffering a presentiment of her deliverance. Theodoret sets the two manifestations in order, that when the sons of God are manifested in their immortality the creation also obtains release; and he cautions that the apostle does not mean the visible creation was really gifted with feeling.

On the groaning Ellicott says that in view of the physical evil prevalent in the world the apostle attributes a human consciousness of pain to the rest of creation, and finds in the figure of travail a reference to the prospect of a joyful delivery. Robertson notes two further compounds formed with the preposition meaning together, both occurring here alone, and says nature is pictured in the pangs of childbirth. Gill makes the same comparison. Clarke turns the verse into an argument for his own reading, asking those who explain the passage of the material world to tell us how that groans and travails, since they must own the phrase borrowed and allusive, whereas on his reading the literal construction may be admitted. Barnes here parts from his own earlier interpretation, taking the whole creation in the natural sense of the word rather than the restricted one he had given before.
23:
Who the ourselves are follows from the reading each gave the creature. Gill and Clarke, who took the earlier verses of the Gentile world, take these of the Jews, Clarke adding that they sigh for the Gentiles' sake, waiting for the redemption of the mystical body of which the Gentiles form so great a part. Barnes and Ellicott take them simply of Christians as distinguished from the creation at large. Theodoret turns the comparison into an argument: what wonder if creation is so affected on our account, when we ourselves, who have received the grace of the Spirit, groan in our longings after freedom? Calvin reports the view that the apostle means to exalt the dignity of our blessedness by showing that all things desire it, but judges rather that a comparison is drawn between the greater and the less.

On the firstfruits Barnes explains that the word denotes the portion of harvest first gathered and consecrated, and so what is first in order of time. Robertson calls it an old metaphor, takes the genitive as one of apposition, and traces the gift from the great Pentecost through the gifts named elsewhere. Ellicott contrasts the first partial outpouring with the plenitude of glory to follow. Wesley identifies the firstfruits with the Spirit himself.

The adoption still to come they explain by what it will bring. Ellicott says we sigh for the time when our adoption will be complete and our mortal bodies transfigured; Theodoret defines it as the redemption of the body. Wesley supplies a Roman custom that gives the word its force: persons privately adopted were brought into the forum and there publicly owned as sons, and so at the general resurrection the sons of God shall be publicly owned.

The clause about being saved by hope Barnes handles with care, denying that hope can be the instrument of salvation. Most commentators, he says, take it to mean that we have as yet attained salvation only in hope; but he suggests that saved may here mean simply that we are kept and preserved. Robertson finds the difficulty in the grammar, since the noun's form is the same for locative, instrumental and dative, and observes that each makes good sense, so that we were saved in hope, by hope, and for hope. Ellicott remarks that it is usually faith rather than hope which is named as the means of salvation. Wesley says our salvation is now only in hope; Theodoret, that we have not attained the resurrection but are comforted by our hopes. Gill answers from another side, that those who have the firstfruits were already saved in the purposes of God and in the hands of Christ.

On the definition that follows Calvin argues from the nature of hope itself: since it extends to things not yet obtained and represents to the mind the form of things hidden and far remote, whatever is openly seen or really possessed cannot be its object; and he uses this to strengthen the exhortation, since our salvation cannot be separated from some kind of death. Clarke agrees that as hope signifies the expectation of future good it supposes its object not yet possessed. Ellicott puts it as a plain consequence: if salvation could be grasped by sight there would be no room for hope, but as it is we do not see it, we hope for it, and therefore endure the sufferings on the road to it. Barnes states the psychology behind the patience: where strong desire is joined to a corresponding expectation there is true hope and a man can wait, whereas desire without expectation produces impatience. Clarke adds that the waiting includes the common ills of life and whatever tribulations the Christian profession brings, since faithful is he who promised. Gill lists what is unseen and yet hoped for: the hour of death, the second coming, the resurrection, eternal glory.
26:
The verb they find inadequately rendered. Clarke says helpeth is far too weak, the word being compounded from the prepositions meaning together and over against, so that it describes one taking hold at the opposite end of a burden and lifting along with us. Robertson calls it a late and striking double compound found in Diodorus and Josephus, occurring only twice in the New Testament, here and in Martha's plea that her sister lend a hand; the apostle, he says, pictures the Holy Spirit taking hold at our side. Barnes gives the same sense, to sustain with us. Ellicott notes that the true reading of the noun is the singular, and marks the balance of the argument, that the prospect of salvation sustains the Christian while the Divine Spirit interposes to aid him. Calvin explains why the help is mentioned: that the faithful might not object that they are too weak to bear so heavy burdens, since none may complain that the cross is beyond his strength when we are sustained by a celestial power.

What our ignorance in prayer consists in they set out carefully. Henry takes it as a weakness both in the matter and the manner, since hope supposes desire and that desire offered to God is prayer, and yet we know not what to pray for as we ought. Wesley enumerates the weaknesses: our understandings weak, particularly in the things of God, our desires weak, our prayers weak. Theodoret draws a rule of practice: ask not to be delivered from affliction, for you do not know what is profitable to you as God your Governor does. Gill sets the help among the Spirit's other offices.

Whose the groanings are divides them. Theodoret says expressly that by the Spirit the apostle means not the Holy Ghost himself but the grace given to the faithful, stirred up by which we pray the more earnestly. Clarke argues the contrary: it is the same Spirit mentioned before as bearing witness with ours, and consequently not a disposition of mind, for the disposition of our mind cannot help the infirmities of our minds. Barnes says the word undoubtedly means the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse to explain the title Comforter, illustrating it from the martyr outraged unjustly with tortures on every side. Wesley finds a boldness in the language, that not only the universe and the children of God but the Spirit himself, as it were, groans. Clarke defines the intercession as made not by supplication on the saints' behalf but by directing their own petitions.

On the searching of hearts they agree that the phrase describes God alone. Gill calls it a periphrasis of God and denies that angels can search the hearts of men, since one man cannot know another's heart nor any man fully know his own. Barnes says it is an attribute incommunicable to a creature, and that God does not need the emotions expressed in words to induce him to hear. Robertson sets the two advocates side by side, the Holy Spirit pleading God's cause with us as Christ is our advocate with the Father, though the Spirit also interprets our prayers. Wesley says God knows the mind of the Spirit though man cannot utter it. Calvin calls the verse a remarkable reason for strengthening our confidence, that we are heard when we pray through his Spirit, since God knows our desires even as he knows the thoughts of his own Spirit; the words about the will of God intimate that he does not regard these emotions as strange nor reject them as unreasonable, but allows them. Ellicott says the same more briefly, that God recognises the voice of his own Spirit because the prayers it prompts accord strictly with his will. Theodoret adds that the apostle writes this from his own experience.
28:
Chrysostom sees the whole passage aimed at men in danger, the sayings about the present sufferings, the groaning creation and salvation by hope having all been mooted with a view to those under persecution. Barnes calls this a fresh source of consolation drawn from the fact that all things are under an infinitely wise Being who has purposed the Christian's salvation. Calvin concludes that so far are the troubles of this life from hindering salvation that they are helps to it. Henry defines the good narrowly: it is good for the saints which does their souls good, every providence tending to break them off from sin. Gill distinguishes a temporal, a spiritual and an eternal good. Clarke lays down two cautions: the persons concerned are they who love God and so live in obedience, and it is not said all things shall work but that they work now for him who loves now. Theodoret makes the restriction sharply: they work not with all but with those that love him, nor simply work but work for good, so that a man who asks what would not profit him fails of his petition.

The text is disputed. Ellicott reports a remarkable reading in the Vatican and Alexandrian manuscripts and in Origen which inserts God as the subject of the verb and makes all things its object, so that God works all things with us, and judges this very early if not original. Robertson notes the same manuscripts and says the idea is the same anyway, since God makes all things work together for an ultimate good. Wesley enumerates what the all things covers, ease or pain, poverty or riches, and the ten thousand changes of life, working strongly and sweetly for spiritual and eternal good.

On the foreknowledge Barnes says the word has been the subject of almost endless disputes: whether it means simply to know that certain persons would become Christians, or to ordain them such. Gill denies that the bare prescience of things future is intended. Ellicott states the case for free-will carefully: foreknowledge does not interfere with it, since though prior in time it is posterior in the order of causation to the act of choice, a man not choosing because a thing is foreknown but it being foreknown because he will choose it. Wesley finds the answer in the words themselves, that those foreknown are the very ones conformable to the image of his Son; Robertson, that this foreknowledge is placed in eternity in the letter to the Ephesians. Calvin takes the conformity as the point of the whole, showing by the order of election that the afflictions of the faithful are nothing else than the manner by which they are conformed to the image of Christ, so that there is no reason to think it hard that we are afflicted unless we would disapprove the Lord's election itself. Cyril of Jerusalem gives the conformity a sacramental ground: baptized into Christ, we have been made conformable to the Son of God, and are properly called anointed.

The chain of verbs Henry calls the order of the causes of our salvation, a golden chain. Gill notes that the predestination is not to sufferings but to grace and glory. Barnes says the apostle states the connexion between predestination and certain salvation because the one implies the other, and takes the calling as effectual, by the Spirit. Clarke reads the whole of the Gentiles, whom God determined to call into his Church with the Jewish people, and notes that all the verbs refer to what had already taken place. Robertson makes the same observation grammatically, the glorification being stated as consummated though still future in the fullest sense; he quotes Sanday and Headlam that the step is complete and certain in the divine counsels. Ellicott admits that predestination seems most of all to interfere with free-will.
31:
They all mark the change of manner. Henry says the apostle closes this discourse with a holy triumph in the name of all the saints, concluding like an orator and speaking as one amazed and swallowed up with the theme. Calvin says the subject being sufficiently proved he now breaks out into exclamations, setting forth the magnanimity with which the faithful ought to be furnished when adversities urge them to despond, and teaching that with the paternal favour of God is joined an invincible courage. Robertson traces the argument from earlier in the chapter as a triumphant presentation reaching its climax in the word glorified, but notes that the apostle now lets the objector have his say, so that the remaining verses take up the objections one by one. Wesley counts the structure: four periods, one general and three particular, each a glorying in the grace of God followed by a question challenging all opponents.

What these things are Gill leaves open, allowing either the afflictions just spoken of, at which we are not to murmur since they work for our good, or the blessings just enumerated. Barnes asks what conclusion follows for the power of the Christian religion to support us in trials. Clarke paraphrases the comfort, that God has called us to holiness and to love of him, and that though persecuted and despised, the doctrines already laid down are our answer.

Theodoret presses the sweep of the challenge. Having God as our ally, shall we be afraid of men? The apostle comprehends all at once under the single word who, whether kings, or generals, or peoples, or their leaders, the whole world at once. Barnes lists the evidence that God is on our side, shown by his adopting us and granting us his Spirit.

The argument from the greater to the less they all recognise. Calvin names it as such, bringing forward the price of our redemption to prove that God favours us. Theodoret puts it in two questions: he has given us the greater, and shall he not give the less? his own Son has he bestowed, and will he deprive us of what we have gained? He adds a christological caution, that the Person of the Son is one, the human nature having been delivered up by the divinity. Clarke frames it as a question about lesser blessings, that if God loved us so as to deliver up his own Son he cannot withhold any minor one, and recalls what was said to Abraham. Henry says that all things in heaven and earth are not so great a display of God's free love as the gift of his coequal Son to be the atonement on the cross, and that all the rest follows upon union with him; he who has prepared a crown for us will give us what we need on the way. Wesley divides the verse into four sentences: God spared not his own Son, therefore he will freely give us all things; he delivered him up for us all, therefore none can lay anything to our charge. The word freely marks that all which follows justification is a free gift also, and the all things whatever is needful or profitable for us.

On the sparing Gill lists what God did not spare: the angels that sinned, the old world, Sodom and Gomorrah, the Egyptians and their firstborn, and Israel itself when it transgressed; none of which is to be wondered at, whereas that he should not spare his own Son is the wonder of the passage. Robertson marks the intensive particle as magnifying the deed, and notes that the verb is the one used of the offering of Isaac; the gift of the Son is both promise and pledge of the all things spoken of earlier. Barnes says the delivering up was the highest proof of love a father could give.
33:
The imagery of the courtroom is agreed. Barnes says the expression is taken from courts of law and asks who shall so charge with crime before God's tribunal as to cause condemnation. Robertson parses the verb as a forensic term for coming forward as an accuser, and observes that Satan is the great Accuser of the brethren while God is the Judge who sets us right, so that the accuser must face the Judge with his charge. Theodoret sets the two questions in sequence: having said that while God helps no one can injure us, the apostle adds that God having justified us no one can condemn.

How the verses should be pointed divides them. Clarke lays them down as pointed by the best Greek critics, so that the answers are themselves questions: who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect, God who justifieth? who is he that condemneth, Christ who died? Ellicott makes a different join, carrying the remainder of the one verse into the next, so that the sense runs, he that died and rose is Christ, who then shall separate us from his love; the two questions, he says, are parts of the reply thrown into interrogative form, the apostle's mind being in an attitude of challenge.

Who the elect are Gill and Wesley take differently. Gill defines them as a certain select number whom God has so loved as of his sovereign good pleasure to choose in Christ before the foundation of the world; and he grants that they are chargeable with Adam's sin and much besides, before answering from the justification that follows. Wesley cites an author for a historical account of the term, that the heathen world revolted and were rejected, while the Jewish nation was chosen and styled the children of God, a holy people, a chosen seed, the elect and the called of God, these titles being given to the whole nation. Barnes takes them as those chosen according to God's eternal purpose, secure because he purposed to save them so that none can bring a charge.

Calvin makes the persuasion itself the ground of everything, since the chief consolation of the godly in adversities is to be fully persuaded of the paternal kindness of God, from which arises the certainty of salvation and that calm quietness of soul through which adversities are sweetened. On the condemning he states the legal principle plainly: as no one by accusing can prevail when the judge absolves, so there remains no condemnation when the penalty is paid, and he who would condemn us must bring Christ himself back to death again.

The four clauses about Christ they distribute among themselves. Barnes suggests the words may be a question, whether Christ who has died shall condemn them, and argues that since he died to save them he will not. Wesley says our faith should not stop at his death but be exercised farther on his resurrection and second coming, and takes the intercession as his presenting there his obedience and our prayers sanctified through him. Clarke explains the session as the exaltation of our human nature, which the Son took into conjunction with his divinity, and the intercession as his managing the concerns of his Church. Robertson calls Christ our Advocate at God's court, who paid the debt for our sins with his blood so that the score is settled. Gill argues from the security of the elect, loved with an everlasting love and in Christ, where there is no condemnation. Cyril of Jerusalem gathers testimonies to the session at the right hand from the Gospel and from Peter and Paul. Theodoret asks what more can be sought, since in our behalf Christ died and having risen sits by the Father, and even so has not ceased his care for us.
35:
Whose love is meant divides them cleanly. Gill says it is not the saints' love to Christ but his love to them, and though their love can never be destroyed but only abated, that is not what is intended. Ellicott states the same in a line. Barnes takes the opposite view openly: the expression is ambiguous and may mean either, but he understands it of our love to Christ. Clarke thinks the question has been generally misunderstood, and refers it to the persecutions to which genuine Christians were exposed through their attachment to Christ. Robertson asks whether anyone can put a distance between Christ's love and us, and notes that the apostle changes from asking who to asking what.

Calvin explains why the conviction now extends even to lower things: he who is persuaded of God's kindness can stand firm in the heaviest afflictions, which harass men because they read them as tokens of God's wrath. Wesley observes that the list proceeds from lesser troubles to greater; Ellicott, that the apostle speaks from his own experience.

On the quotation Barnes says it is cited not as originally referring to Christians but as aptly descriptive of their condition. Ellicott dates the psalm to a period of great national distress, probably not earlier than Josiah, and adds that the sufferings of God's people at all times are typical of each other. Calvin says the dread of death is so far from being a reason for falling away that it has almost always been the lot of God's servants to have death before their eyes. Clarke says these things are no more than we may expect from the constitution of the world and the predictions of the prophet. Theodoret says the witness is exactly correspondent to the subject, being spoken in the persons of men with the same object. Gill applies it to Old Testament saints put to death for the worship of God.

The compound in the next verse they linger over. Robertson calls it a late and rare formation occurring here alone in the New Testament, and renders it that we gain a surpassing victory through the one who loved us. Calvin says he has retained the apostle's own word, reports the renderings of others, and notes the intensive force of the preposition. Barnes explains the victory as meaning that these things have no power to subdue us or produce apostasy. Ellicott says that so far from being vanquished we are conquerors, and that when we are weak then are we strong. Wesley says we are not only no losers but abundant gainers by all these trials. Clarke draws the answer from the psalm itself, that as the prophet added that all this had come upon them yet they had not dealt falsely in his covenant, so we abide faithful. Theodoret grounds the victory on a comparison, that it were most absurd for Christ to have undergone death for sinners and for ourselves not readily to embrace martyrdom for him.

On the persuasion Robertson parses the perfect and renders it that he stands convinced, the items named being those which people dread. Barnes says the expression implies unwavering certainty, and expounds the first pair as neither the fear of death nor the hope of life. Ellicott says the enumeration is meant to include, poetically rather than logically, every possible category of being, especially the unseen powers of evil against which the Christian warfare is directed. Gill says the persuasion regards not himself only but others, and is not conjectural but certain. Cyril of Jerusalem puts the verse in the mouth of the believer facing the last adversary: the Lord, knowing the greatness of that enemy, permits flight to the mountains, but whoever is stout-hearted enough to encounter him may stand and say, who shall separate us from the love of Christ.
